newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Russia says ready to open talks with NATO.
newsitem.headline: Russia says ready to open talks with NATO.

text.p: Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov said on Wednesday Moscow had agreed to an offer from NATO to open talks on a special relationship, but reiterated Russia's opposition to the alliance's plans to expand eastwards.

"We were made an offer to hold consultations with NATO in order to settle any issues that might be of concern to us. We agreed to this offer. I think this will open the door to fruitful talks," Primakov told a news conference after a meeting with the 16 NATO foreign ministers.
Primakov, standing alongside a beaming NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana, quickly added that Russia had not altered its stand against the alliance's enlargement plans.

"I would like to underline that we are sticking to our negative position towards the enlargement of NATO," Primakov said. "This is based on the firm belief that it will inevitably lead to a new division of Europe. That is unacceptable."

Moscow, which has long protested that NATO enlargement would endanger its security, has indicated thay it does not want the issue to stand in the way of it negotiating a charter covering all aspects of its relations with its former Cold War foe.
Primakov said the charter should be far more than just a general set of principles and contain "very specific, very concrete" points addressing Moscow's security concerns.
Primakov gave no indication of when he thought talks on the treaty might start.

NATO, which wants the negotiations with Russia to be sealed at a July summit called to name the first new NATO members, has authorised Solana to open talks, but member states have yet to agree his precise negotiating brief.
Solana described his meeting with Primakov as "cordial" and again stressed the alliance's desire to have a solid working relationship with Moscow.
"Security in Europe cannot be established without Russia," he told reporters.
Initial reactions to Primakov's visit were favourable.
"We were surprised and delighted by Russia's constructive attitude," said German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel.

"It is interesting that they (the Russians) are now indicating a willingness to talk to us on the essentials. They are no longer asking us to change the enlargement policy before they can talk," a NATO official told reporters on Tuesday.
Some diplomats said Primakov's apparent eagerness to start talks might sow mischief, since NATO members had yet to agree among themselves what kind of deal the alliance could offer Russia.

NATO foreign ministers on Tuesday set July 8-9 for a special enlargement summit in Madrid to name its first new members from former communist Europe and the first new additions for more than 25 years.
The Czech Republic, Hungary and Poland are on most observers' lists of favourites.
The trickiest issue facing NATO is how to work out a charter or even treaty on future ties with Russia while trying to persuade Moscow that the alliance has no hostile intentions.

U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher vowed NATO would not station nuclear missiles on the territory of new members, but Moscow is more interested in the concessions it can wring from its old foe.
Defence officials say one possibility would be to form a new structure which might give Moscow some influence in how the alliance was run.
